when: a GPU-side operation that can run while device memory or the KV pool is nearly full allocates temporaries whose size scales with the request or data size
expect: Ask the author to report the peak extra device memory for a long request. If it is unbounded or large, ask them to process the work in chunks with a fixed byte cap. Any ordering guarantee the unchunked version relied on must still hold across chunk boundaries, and a test must verify the chunked result matches the unchunked one.
why: Temporaries proportional to request size can OOM exactly when memory is scarcest, and naive chunking can break overlap or ordering assumptions.
examples: KV compaction or block-move gather allocating a buffer sized to a 128K-token request; chunk under a byte cap and ensure earlier destinations never overwrite later sources
a gather kernel that materializes all selected blocks at once instead of in capped batches
concern: Bound GPU temporary memory in KV operations under pool pressure (chunk with byte cap, preserve ordering)

when: code writes in place into paged KV cache blocks owned by the serving engine
expect: Ask for exclusive block ownership to be documented as an explicit precondition of the writing function. Check that every caller guarantees the blocks are private before writing, either by copy-on-write or by excluding those requests from prefix caching.
why: With prefix caching, the engine may share one physical KV block among several requests, so an in-place write silently corrupts other requests' KV.
examples: a function that compacts or relocates KV inside vLLM paged blocks without checking whether a block is shared via the prefix cache
concern: In-place writes to paged KV blocks must ensure exclusive ownership (prefix-cache sharing)

when: a change alters LMCache behavior to compensate for how an upstream engine reports or handles state
expect: Ask the PR description to state the upstream semantics being relied on, including what the engine is expected to report and why the observed behavior deviates from it. It must also justify why the fix belongs in LMCache rather than upstream, or link an upstream issue or PR.
why: Undocumented workarounds encode assumptions about upstream behavior that break silently when upstream changes, and they may hide an upstream bug.
examples: filtering load-only requests out of vLLM's finished_sending, where only requests that performed a store should appear
concern: Justify vLLM-semantics workarounds in LMCache and why not fixed upstream

when: a docstring explains in prose a multi-step or non-obvious state transformation that the reader has to simulate in their head
expect: Ask for a self-contained worked example in the docstring that shows the initial state, the arguments of successive calls, and the resulting state after each call.
why: Prose alone for stateful transformations is ambiguous and hard to verify, while a concrete trace makes both intent and bugs visible.
examples: a function tracking block ids under speculative relocation, documented only in prose
concern: Docstrings for non-obvious state changes need a worked example

when: a reconnection or recovery path restores a connection to a peer that negotiated parameters during the initial handshake
expect: Check that recovery re-runs the full handshake negotiation, not just resource re-registration. It must verify every renegotiated parameter against the values the local side cached, and only then mark the connection healthy or re-register resources. Mismatches must be handled explicitly.
why: A restarted peer comes back with its configured defaults while the local side still holds previously negotiated values, which leads to silent inconsistency.
examples: vLLM multiprocess adapter reconnecting to a restarted LMCache server that only re-registers KV and never renegotiates chunk size
concern: Recovery/reconnect must re-run handshake negotiation and verify before marking healthy
